To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the reduced Ca2+ sensitivity and reduced maximum force per CSA in ischemic fibers are best described as a reduced rate of transition between A-M.ADP and AM*.ADP states, which may be mediated by reduced TnT and Ser23/24 TnI phosphorylations.
the rate of initial crossbridge activation in rat heart muscle is reduced during ischemia, possibly as a result of reduced TnI and TnT phosphorylation.

the reduced contractility of ischemic rat hearts can be described as a reduced rate of crossbridge activation, and that this reduction in activation rate is likely mediated by reduced TnT and increased TnI phosphorylations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of muscle contraction.
understanding the mechanisms of heart failure and the development of new therapeutic strategies to treat this disease.
the molecular mechanisms of myocardial contractility and relaxation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ischemia alters the kinetics of the crossbridge activation cycle by reducing the forward rate constant for the isomerization between A-M.ADP and AM*.ADP, and that this is mediated by changes in the post-translinal state of TnT.
the crossbridge cycle is affected by ischemia in a manner that is commensurate to the changes in the phosphorylation status of TnT and Ser23/24 of TnI.
ischemic heart failure is characterized by a reduction of the rate of crossbridge activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified an altered crossbridge cycle that is commensurate to the altered contractility in ischemic fibers and that this altered crossbridge cycle is mediated by changes in the post-translional state of TnI.
ischemic conditions reduce the forward rate of the transition between A-M.ADP-Pi to AM*.DPi, and that this transition is associated with the activation of thin filaments.
the altered contractile response of the heart to ischemia may result, in part, from an altered crossbridge cycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate of activation from the noncycling to cycling crossbridge states is reduced during ischemia, and that this change may be mediated by the post-translative state of troponins T and I.

ischemic injury reduces the rate constant of the initial transition in the actomysoin crossbridge cycle that underlies the generation of tension, and that this alteration is mediated by changes in TnT and/or TnI phosphorylations.

the changes in the actin-myosin crossbridge cycling that occur in the ischemic heart are not well understood, but that the crossbridge cycle can be used to describe and explain the changes in contractility that occur in the setting of ischemia.
